title: SchemaRegistry singleton has unlocked dict caches racing with clear_cache()
design:
Thread-safety audit finding (polylogue-xikl lane, 2026-07-19).

`SchemaRegistry` (polylogue/schemas/runtime_registry.py:237-250) holds three
plain, unlocked instance dicts mutated via classic check-then-set:
`_catalog_cache`, `_schema_cache`, `_workload_profile_cache`
(`load_package_catalog` ~line 293, `get_element_schema` ~line 828,
`resolve_payload` ~line 749). It is instantiated as a process-wide singleton
through TWO independent unlocked global caching call-sites that both feed the
parse path:

- `polylogue/pipeline/services/ingest_worker.py:44,152-159`
  (`_SCHEMA_REGISTRY` module global, `_runtime_schema_registry()`
  check-then-set, no lock) -- called from `_resolve_plan_schema` at
  `ingest_worker.py:225`, invoked per record during parse
  (`_schema_payload_for_artifact` -> `resolve_payload`).
- `polylogue/schemas/validator_resolution.py:25` (`_shared_registry`,
  `@lru_cache(maxsize=8)`) -- a second, independent path to the SAME class
  reachable from validation/backfill code.

Hazard shape: `save_package_catalog()` calls `self.clear_cache()` (dict
`.clear()` on all three caches) with no lock. A concurrent reader doing
`if cache_key in self._schema_cache: return self._schema_cache[cache_key]`
can have the `.clear()` land between the `in` check and the `[key]` access,
raising an uncaught `KeyError` -- a genuine crash, not just wasted work.
Independently, concurrent misses on the same key cause redundant catalog
file reads + JSON parse + object construction (benign waste, but real cache
thrashing under N parse threads).

This directly blocks polylogue-xikl phase 2 (parse path on
ThreadPoolExecutor): schema resolution runs inside every eligible parse
record today, so parallel parse threads will call `resolve_payload`/
`get_element_schema` on the same shared, unlocked `SchemaRegistry` instance
concurrently.

Remediation shape (pick one): (a) add a `threading.Lock` around all three
cache dicts' read-check-write and around `clear_cache()`; (b) make the
caches populate-once-immutable per catalog load (compute once under lock,
publish an immutable mapping) so plain reads need no lock afterward; (c)
give each parse thread its own `SchemaRegistry` instance (loses cross-thread
cache reuse, simplest). (a) or (b) preserve today's cross-request cache
reuse; recommend (b) since catalogs are read-mostly and rarely invalidated
(`save_package_catalog` is an admin/maintenance path, not a hot path).

Not yet verified: whether `save_package_catalog`/`clear_cache()` is ever
called concurrently with parse in production today (it looks like an
admin/schema-authoring path, `devtools lab` tooling), so this is scoped as
a *design hazard that blocks the planned parse-parallelization*, not a
currently-observed production crash. Flagged as its own bead per the
audit's severity trigger because the failure mode (KeyError under simple
dict-clear-during-check-then-set) is concrete and easy to trigger with a
`ThreadPoolExecutor` fuzz test, not merely theoretical.
acceptance_criteria: SchemaRegistry's _catalog_cache/_schema_cache/_workload_profile_cache are protected against concurrent read/clear races (lock, immutable-publish, or per-thread instance); a ThreadPoolExecutor-based regression test reproduces the KeyError-under-clear race before the fix and passes after; both call sites (ingest_worker._runtime_schema_registry, validator_resolution._shared_registry) converge on the same safe pattern
notes:
2026-07-19 Implemented in feature/fix/thread-safety-hardening-wave-1 (commit
adbb184f6), lane worktree agent-a56d7844ed5bb9547.

Fix shape: added SchemaRegistry._cache_lock (threading.Lock), guarding
read-check/populate of _catalog_cache/_schema_cache/_workload_profile_cache
and clear_cache(). Construction of cache values (file I/O, JSON parse) stays
outside the lock so parallel parse threads never block on each other's I/O,
only on the cheap dict access -- a redundant miss just re-does the (idempotent)
load. Both entry points converge on the same safe pattern per AC:
ingest_worker.py's _runtime_schema_registry() now uses its own module-level
lock around its check-then-set on _SCHEMA_REGISTRY; validator_resolution.py's
_shared_registry() was already safe as-is (functools.lru_cache has its own
internal lock, documented thread-safe) and needed no change -- the shared
hazard was entirely inside the SchemaRegistry instance's own caches, which the
lock now covers regardless of which entry point handed out the reference.

Test: tests/unit/core/test_runtime_registry_helpers.py::
test_concurrent_schema_reads_survive_concurrent_clear_cache. Anti-vacuity:
swapped the three cache dicts for a dict subclass whose __contains__ sleeps
*after* a positive membership check (widening the check-then-get window
deterministically rather than relying on iteration-count luck). Reverting the
production fix reproduces KeyError(('chatgpt','v1',None)) on every run against
this test (verified via git diff/checkout/apply, not stash); with the fix
applied it passes reliably. A second test,
tests/unit/pipeline/test_ingest_worker_assembly.py::
test_runtime_schema_registry_singleton_is_race_safe_under_concurrent_first_access,
proves the ingest_worker singleton constructs exactly one SchemaRegistry under
8 concurrent first-access threads (reverting reproduces 8 distinct instances,
confirmed).

AC status: cache dicts protected (lock) -- satisfied. ThreadPoolExecutor-based
regression test reproducing the pre-fix KeyError -- satisfied (via the slow-
dict seam, not raw iteration count, since raw iteration count alone did not
reproduce it reliably in practice). Both call sites converge on a safe
pattern -- satisfied (lock for ingest_worker's own singleton; lru_cache was
already safe; the shared SchemaRegistry-instance hazard is closed either way).

PR not yet opened at note time; see the epic bead / commit history on
feature/fix/thread-safety-hardening-wave-1 for current state. Not closing --
coordinator closes after merge.
PR opened: https://github.com/Sinity/polylogue/pull/3154 (branch feature/fix/thread-safety-hardening-wave-1). Not closing -- coordinator closes after merge.
close_reason: Merged in PR #3154: SchemaRegistry cache dicts + ingest_worker singleton lock-guarded (double-checked pattern, construction outside lock); deterministic race test proven to fail pre-fix via patch-revert.

title: Free-threading adoption program: 3.14/3.14t across polylogue
design: Operator decision 2026-07-19: adopt free-threaded Python across polylogue, fully. Phases: (0) 3.13->3.14 migration on the standard build (flake python version, pyproject requires-python, uv.lock, deprecation sweep, suite green) — prerequisite, its own PR; (1) 3.14t experiment gate (child: the 7mtf bead — devshell lane, suite classification under free-threading, parse benchmarks incl. daemon-shaped concurrent-writer scenario); (2) adoption wave: ThreadPoolExecutor parse in census+ingest (retires process_pool.py, _census_parse_worker, size partition, amortization floor, the p0pw hazard class), convergence redesign with parse outside writer holds + in-daemon blue-green builds (child: m6tp option b), read-path per-request parallelism (MCP/HTTP hydration), insight materialization fan-out, render/export fan-out; (3) thread-safety audit feeding all of phase 2 (shared mutable state inventory: module caches, parser state, write-path signature caches stay writer-thread-owned). Full opportunity map + costs recorded on the 7mtf bead 2026-07-19. polylogue-9as9 (GIL-world executor workaround) is conditional: re-scope or close once the gate passes. Deployment edge: CLI/offline rebuild adopts 3.14t first (separate process, zero daemon blast radius), daemon second after the gate + audit.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The adoption decision recorded on 2026-07-19 is executed, not re-litigated: polylogue runs on free-threaded 3.14t as the supported runtime. 2. Every module that assumed GIL-serialized access is audited and either proven safe or explicitly locked; the audit names what was checked. 3. A concurrency regression suite exercises the parallel paths that motivated adoption (census parse, watcher chunks) under 3.14t. 4. Packaging, CI, and the deployed daemon all run the same interpreter build; no path silently falls back to GIL-enabled 3.14.
notes:
2026-07-19 (war-room lane, nix wrapper follow-up): Verified + fixed the "bin
wrapper must scrub PYTHONPATH" follow-up filed at 17:10 (PR #3162's own
merge, 46c11a4b6, already landed the PYTHONPATH/PYTHONHOME/PYTHONBREAKPOINT/
PYTHONUSERBASE/VIRTUAL_ENV unset in mkPolylogue's shared postFixup -- covers
both `polylogue` and `polylogue-freethreaded` since they call the same
function). Reproduced the reported failure anyway: with that fix in place,
`polylogue status`/`demo seed` STILL failed under this repo's own ambient
3.13 devshell environment with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'_sysconfigdata__linux_x86_64-linux-gnu'` -- but only for commands doing
real work (--version/--help short-circuit before hitting the failing path,
which is why the original fix looked sufficient).

Bisected with `env -i` (adding exactly one inherited var back at a time):
PYTHONPATH alone does NOT reproduce it. The actual trigger is
`_PYTHON_SYSCONFIGDATA_NAME`, a nixpkgs-set env var that Python's own
`sysconfig._get_sysconfigdata_name()` trusts over its own computation when
present in the environment. Confirmed via `find .../lib/python3.14t -iname
'_sysconfigdata*'`: the free-threaded build's real module carries a `t`
abiflag segment (`_sysconfigdata_t_linux_x86_64-linux-gnu`), but a
3.13-devshell-derived value of this env var
(`_sysconfigdata__linux_x86_64-linux-gnu`, no `t`) doesn't match it -- hence
ModuleNotFoundError, not "wrong version picked up". None of the existing
--unset flags covered this var.

Fix: added `--unset _PYTHON_SYSCONFIGDATA_NAME --unset _PYTHON_HOST_PLATFORM`
(the sibling nixpkgs var for the same leak class, added defensively) to all
three wrapper sites in flake.nix -- mkPolylogue's postFixup (both packages)
and polylogueApiPythonWrapped's raw-interpreter wrapper.

Verification: `nix build .#polylogue-freethreaded` and `.#polylogue` both
succeed; with this session's actual ambient devshell env still exported
(PYTHONPATH at the 3.13 venv site-packages + both nixpkgs vars as they're
really set), both packages' `polylogue demo seed` + `polylogue demo verify`
complete successfully end-to-end (16 sessions/62 messages/4 query hits,
exercising the real msgspec-JSON-backend + sqlite ingest/FTS path, not just
--version).

title: Multi-core census parse: pass-scoped warm executor + worker-side result lowering
design: Operator question 2026-07-19: why is the rebuild single-core on a 24-thread machine? Answer: GIL rules out threads for pure-python parse (processes required); #3136 measured pool dispatch at 0.63x for >256KiB payloads (pickling ParsedSession graphs back exceeds parse savings) so large raws are sequential; #3149 floor made small batches sequential too (per-call executors + ~1.5s spawn import tax per worker = ~95% overhead on 2-raw census batches, measured via py-spy --subprocesses). Neither blocker is fundamental. Implementation plan, two stages: (1) PASS-SCOPED EXECUTOR — create one ProcessPoolExecutor at the top of backfill_historical_revision_evidence (and the daemon census entry), thread it down to _parse_retained_raws (parameter, None = current per-call behavior); with warm workers the spawn tax amortizes to ~12s per multi-minute page and the #3149 floor should then be bypassed when a warm pool is provided (the floor exists ONLY because of per-call spawn cost; small-payload pool dispatch was a measured 1.22x win even INCLUDING spawn). Executor lifecycle: create lazily on first pool-eligible batch, shutdown in finally; do NOT keep a module-global (daemon memory: 8 idle spawn workers with polylogue imported ~0.5GB RSS). (2) WORKER-SIDE LOWERING — the big lever: _census_parse_worker returns compact rows (e.g. pre-serialized session tuples or a spill file path the parent bulk-reads) instead of ParsedSession object graphs, killing the pickle-back cost that makes >256KiB payloads pool-ineligible; then whales parse across all cores (est. 3-5x census phase; parse measured ~50% of census wall). Alternative cheap win if (2) is deferred: pipeline prefetch (parse cohort N+1 in one worker while the writer writes N). COORDINATION: touches sources/revision_backfill.py — do not start until the FTS bulk-mode lane (crd8, in flight 2026-07-19) merges; rebase over it. Benchmark before/after with tests/infra/revision_backfill_benchmark.py SMALL and LARGE shapes plus a warm-pool variant; anti-vacuity via patch-revert (never git stash — refs/stash is worktree-shared).
acceptance_criteria: Warm-pool small-batch dispatch beats sequential on the benchmark (the 1.22x class, without spawn overhead); large-payload parallel parse beats sequential after lowering (report ratio); daemon path unaffected unless explicitly wired; floor logic updated coherently with a comment explaining the new economics; no executor leaks (test: process count returns to baseline after backfill).
notes:
2026-07-19: cross-ref — free-threaded 3.14t research filed (see the 3.14t experiment bead): under free-threading, threads share ParsedSession objects by reference, eliminating both measured blockers this bead works around (pickle-back 0.63x, spawn import tax). If the 3.14t experiment wins its gate, prefer that path for the bulk rebuild and re-scope this bead to the daemon/standard-build world or close it.
2026-07-19 (polylogue-7mtf gate outcome): the 3.14t free-threading experiment
gate PASSED with a wide margin (LARGE-shape ThreadPoolExecutor parse 3.9x-9.6x
speedup at 4-16 workers vs 7.7% single-thread tax; full table + daemon-shaped
writer-starvation finding on polylogue-7mtf). Per that bead's own acceptance
criteria ("polylogue-9as9 re-scoped or closed against the outcome"),
DECISION: stay OPEN, as currently scoped -- do NOT close or re-scope yet.

Reason: the gate passing is necessary but not sufficient for adoption.
polylogue-7mtf also surfaced a NEW hard blocker not in the original research:
orjson (hard runtime dependency) ships zero cp314t wheels at any version and
its own build explicitly refuses to compile under free-threaded Python
("orjson does not support free-threaded Python", verified against 3.11.9).
orjson is imported unconditionally in polylogue/core/json.py, transitively
required by the whole parse path. Concretely: polylogue cannot run on 3.14t
at all today without a throwaway JSON shim (used only to make the 7mtf
experiment's benchmarks executable, never a production answer). Until that
blocker clears -- either an upstream orjson cp314t release or a deliberate
wire-JSON library swap decision -- this bead's standard-build (GIL) executor
workaround remains the only deployable path for census/backfill parse
parallelism, so it should not be closed or narrowed based on the free-
threading gate alone.

Revisit when: an upstream orjson cp314t wheel exists, or a decision is made
to replace/shim orjson for a real (non-experiment) 3.14t deployment.
2026-07-19 disposition update (polylogue-xikl.4 lane, Ref polylogue-xikl):
this bead's own orjson-blocker rationale for staying open has been partly
overtaken by events since it was written earlier today. Two things changed:

1. polylogue-xikl.3 (PR #3155, merged) optionalized orjson via a 3-tier
   core/json.py facade (orjson -> msgspec -> stdlib). Verified live this
   session: a real nixpkgs#python314FreeThreading venv with orjson
   deliberately UNINSTALLED (msgspec + everything else from pyproject
   installed normally, no shim) runs polylogue's revision_backfill/
   process_pool test modules cleanly -- polylogue now genuinely runs on
   3.14t today, not merely "would run once orjson ships a wheel". The
   "polylogue cannot run on 3.14t at all today" premise this bead's
   2026-07-19 note relied on to justify staying open is no longer true.
2. polylogue-xikl.4 (this lane) landed the actual adoption-wave deliverable
   this bead's own notes anticipated: `_parse_unique_retained_raws` in
   sources/revision_backfill.py now dispatches parse across a
   ThreadPoolExecutor whenever `parallel_threads_effective()` (a new
   sys._is_gil_enabled()-based probe) is true, with NO size partition and
   NO amortization floor -- both of which existed solely to amortize this
   bead's own two named costs (process-pool pickle-back #3136, spawn+import
   tax #3149). On a real free-threaded interpreter those costs simply don't
   exist for threads, so this bead's proposed "PASS-SCOPED EXECUTOR +
   WORKER-SIDE LOWERING" design is now the wrong lever for that world: no
   pass-scoped warm ProcessPoolExecutor and no worker-side result lowering
   would beat what free-threading already gives for free.

RECOMMENDATION: re-scope, do not close. The daemon has NOT yet moved to
3.14t (per the epic's own "Deployment edge": CLI/offline rebuild adopts
3.14t first, daemon only after the thread-safety audit + an explicit gate
decision) -- the standard GIL build remains what's actually deployed today,
and my new thread path is a documented no-op there by design (gated
specifically OFF under a real GIL, per the 7mtf control-run's ~5000x
writer-starvation finding). This bead's warm-pool + worker-side-lowering
design still has real, if narrowing, standalone value for THAT deployed
GIL-build daemon in the meantime. Recommend narrowing this bead's scope
explicitly to "GIL-build-only census parse throughput, valid only until the
daemon itself migrates to 3.14t" rather than closing it outright -- closing
would discard a legitimate near-term win with no cost-free way to recover
the design later. Leaving priority/AC/design untouched pending an explicit
operator/coordinator call on whether the GIL-build daemon's spawn-tax pain
is worth solving before the 3.14t daemon migration lands (which would make
this bead moot on its own timeline instead of by architecture).
close_reason: Coordinator call 2026-07-19: moot by architecture — the GIL-build spawn-tax problem this bead solves disappears when polylogue-dcz5 (3.14t daemon deploy, m6tp phase b) lands; thread fan-outs are already runtime-gated (#3161/#3167/#3168). Reopen only if the 3.14t daemon deploy is rejected.

title: Census/parse dedup by blob_hash: 8.7GB (17%) of newest-only bytes are byte-identical duplicate blobs parsed repeatedly
design: Evidence (2026-07-19, live source.db): newest-revision-per-logical_source_key = 87,177 rows / 52.1GB, but only 85,066 DISTINCT blob_hashes / 43.4GB — the same bytes (e.g. one 442MB codex computer-use rollout) appear under up to 8 different logical_source_keys and get fully parsed+censused once per row. The blob store already dedups storage by hash; the census/parse layer does not. Fix direction: memoize census/parse outcomes by (blob_hash, parser fingerprint) — when a second raw row references an already-censused blob, copy/bind the census result (logical keys need care: same bytes under different source_path may legitimately yield different workspace-scoped native ids for some providers — audit which parsers use source_path in identity (e.g. beads workspace ids do!) and scope the memo to providers whose parse is source_path-independent, or key the memo by (blob_hash, fingerprint, identity-relevant path component). Interaction: lane I byte-proof skip (#3146) handles superseded-in-cohort; this handles cross-cohort identical bytes. Ref polylogue-6mvg umbrella.
acceptance_criteria: Byte-identical blobs are parsed at most once per parser fingerprint (per identity-relevant path scope); measured on a corpus with duplicated blobs; no identity regression for source_path-dependent parsers (test covers the beads workspace case).
close_reason: Fixed in PR #3234 (merged b3429fae6): _parse_retained_raws dedup key widened to (provider, blob_hash) for the audited _PATH_INDEPENDENT_PARSE_PROVIDERS allowlist (Beads/Antigravity/Hermes/UNKNOWN excluded — path-derived identity documented per provider). Measured receipt: 200→40 parse calls, 0.516s→0.104s (40 distinct 300KB payloads × 5 paths). Live evidence: 87,177 newest-revision raws / 52.1 GiB vs 85,066 distinct blobs / 43.4 GiB.

title: Prefix-tail rewrite of whale lineage sessions detonates per-row FTS/trigram delete maintenance: single DELETE read 450GB+
design: Found live 2026-07-19 05:00-05:20 on the emergency rebuild: session/message counters flat for 15+ min; py-spy showed 100% of samples inside ONE conn.execute in _delete_prefix_message_dependents (storage/sqlite/archive_tiers/write.py:4195, the per-table DELETE loop) under _reextract_prefix_tail_db -> _resolve_session_graph -> write_parsed_session_to_archive; /proc IO sampling: 585 MB/s sustained reads, 0 writes, ~24% CPU — cumulative process read_bytes 1.67TB. The derived_refresh_guard IS correctly scoped (action_pairs/delegation triggers do not fire), and the visible per-row triggers are individually cheap EXCEPT blocks_command_trigram_ad: the external-content-style delete (INSERT INTO blocks_command_trigram(blocks_command_trigram, rowid, tool_detail_text) VALUES (delete, ...)) re-tokenizes each deleted tool_use command and removes per-trigram postings — for a whale prefix (10K+ tool blocks x long command texts x hundreds of trigrams each) this is millions of scattered posting-list page reads over a multi-GB trigram index. messages_fts contentless_delete may contribute similarly. Every prefix-sharing lineage session (fork/resume/compaction) with a large prefix pays this on EVERY full re-write, in daemon live ingest as well as bulk rebuild. Measure with the revision_backfill benchmark extended by a trigram-heavy whale-lineage corpus shape.

title: Fresh index generations run unanalyzed: planner picks global block_type index, O(N^2) replay writes
design: Found live 2026-07-19 during the emergency rebuild: replay phase spent 72% of CPU in refresh_action_pairs (py-spy, 5912 samples). EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the running generation showed all three subqueries of action_pairs_refresh_sql using SEARCH u USING INDEX idx_blocks_type_tool (block_type=?) with session_id as residual filter — every per-session refresh scanned ALL 181K tool_use blocks in the archive (plus a per-row messages join), three times. Cause: a freshly bootstrapped generation has NO sqlite_stat1 (never ANALYZEd), and without stats the planner prefers the block_type equality index (94,629 rows/key) over idx_blocks_session_position (333 rows/key). Production index.db has stat1 (PRAGMA optimize wired in schema.py/maintenance.py) so steady-state is mostly fine — but EVERY fresh tier build (ops maintenance rebuild-index generations, ops reset --index + daemon rebuild, first bootstrap) runs its entire bulk phase on the unanalyzed db. Live mitigation applied tonight: manual ANALYZE on the in-flight generation (20.2s, slotted between batch commits) — planner immediately flipped to idx_blocks_session_position on all subqueries. Fix directions (both): (1) run ANALYZE (or targeted ANALYZE blocks/messages/action_pairs) in generation bootstrap right after DDL creation AND periodically during bulk replay (e.g. every N thousand sessions, stats drift as tables grow from 0); (2) consider planner-steering the hot writer SQL (unary-plus on block_type, or INDEXED BY idx_blocks_session_position) so writer-path plans never depend on stats freshness — deterministic beats statistical for per-session maintenance queries. Also audit other writer-path session-scoped queries for the same trap (any WHERE session_id=? AND <indexed-equality-col>).
acceptance_criteria: Fresh-generation bootstrap produces correct plans for action_pairs_refresh_sql from the first write (test: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN asserts idx_blocks_session_position on an empty freshly-bootstrapped index); bulk rebuild re-analyzes as tables grow; decision recorded on deterministic steering vs stats; measured before/after on the rebuild benchmark.
notes: 2026-07-19 04:00 measured impact of the live mitigation (manual ANALYZE on the in-flight generation at ~03:55): replay throughput jumped from ~2.9 sessions/min (03:36-03:54 window) to ~60 sessions/min sustained (03:55:59-03:58:25: +146 sessions, +134,217 messages in 146s ≈ 55K messages/min) — >20x sessions-rate, ~90x message-rate on the write path. Confirms the O(N^2) diagnosis: refresh_action_pairs was scanning all archive tool_use blocks per session write via idx_blocks_type_tool; post-ANALYZE plan uses idx_blocks_session_position. Note: bootstrap already calls PRAGMA optimize (schema.py:65) but on an EMPTY db it is a no-op — the fix must analyze AFTER data exists (periodic during bulk, or deterministic planner steering).
close_reason: Merged as PR #3141 (2ea211bee): PLANNER_STAT1_SEED_SQL at create_fresh (sync+async) + bounded per-page ANALYZE in rebuild_index. Live measurement on the emergency rebuild: manual equivalent gave >20x sustained replay speedup (2.9 -> 60 sessions/min). Deterministic unary-plus steering of action_pairs_refresh_sql recorded as future option (trigger-DDL-embedded = derived schema bump). Writer-path session-scoped query audit spun off implicitly to 6mvg umbrella.

title: Identity-hash pipeline burns ~32% of census CPU: session tree serialized multiple times per revision
design: py-spy profile of the live 2026-07-19 rebuild (5912 samples, sequential parse): hash_payload = 32% cumulative, json dumps/iterencode = 27%/25% (C encoder IS active — measured; this is real serializer volume, not a pure-python fallback), while actual codex parse_stream = 49%. Cause: session_revision_projection (pipeline/ids.py:186) serializes every message payload individually AND session_content_hash re-serializes the entire session again — the tree is JSON-encoded at least twice per revision, then SHA-256d, for all 101K revisions including the 46% superseded ones. Directions, cheapest-first: (a) reuse per-message hashes in the session hash (Merkle: session hash over message-hash list + normalized header) — halves serialization volume but CHANGES persisted hash values; (b) faster canonical serializer (orjson, pre-built wheel) — also changes bytes (ensure_ascii vs raw UTF-8); (c) cache projection per (raw blob_hash, parser fingerprint) so re-census never re-hashes unchanged revisions. CONSTRAINT: these hashes land in durable source.db revision evidence (bind_source_raw_revision) — any byte-definition change is an evidence epoch: needs an explicit migration/epoch decision, not a silent swap. (c) is epoch-free and may be the right first move. Benchmark harness exists: tests/infra/revision_backfill_benchmark.py (from #3136).
acceptance_criteria: Decision recorded (epoch vs cache-first); implementation cuts census-phase hash CPU share measurably on the benchmark (before/after numbers in PR); durable-evidence compatibility explicitly addressed; no silent identity-hash change.
notes:
## Lane J decision — hash economics (2026-07-19)

**Benchmark** (`tests/infra/hash_economics_benchmark.py`, synthetic sessions w/
tool_use+tool_input, attachments, session_events; median of 7 passes x 20
sessions):

| candidate | epoch? | 100 msg | 300 msg | 800 msg |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| status quo (pre-fix) | - | 1134us | 3016us | 7503us |
| **dedup (SHIPPED)** | **no** | 959us (-15.5%) | 2586us (-14.2%) | 6483us (-13.6%) |
| merkle (session_hash from message-hash list) | yes | 720us (-36.6%) | 1901us (-37.0%) | 4815us (-35.8%) |
| orjson (swap stdlib json.dumps) | yes | 333us (-70.6%) | 983us (-67.4%) | 2543us (-66.1%) |
| dedup+merkle+orjson (ceiling) | yes | 284us (-74.9%) | 812us (-73.1%) | 2157us (-71.3%) |

**Standout finding, contrary to the bead's cheapest-first ordering:** orjson
alone beats merkle by ~2x (67-71% vs 35-37% savings) — it's the dominant
lever, not the whole-tree-reserialization elimination. Root cause: orjson's C
serializer is intrinsically faster per byte than stdlib json even for
equivalent work; it doesn't need the Merkle restructuring to win big. Any
future epoch-gated pass should prioritize orjson over/alongside merkle.

**Consumer map** (durable vs rebuildable): `session_hash` lands in TWO tiers —
durable `source.db` (`raw_session_memberships.normalized_content_hash` BLOB,
`raw_sessions.source_revision` via `bind_source_raw_revision`,
`storage/sqlite/archive_tiers/source_write.py:650`) and rebuildable
`index.db` (`sessions.content_hash`, `storage/sqlite/archive_tiers/write.py`).
The durable side is the real epoch constraint — everything else
(`repair.py`, `raw_reconciler.py`, `archive.py` comparisons) computes fresh
and compares against one of these two stored forms. The existing
`parser_fingerprint='revision-membership-v1'` census-receipt scheme
(`raw_authority_parser_census`, keyed by (raw_id, fingerprint)) is already the
clean invalidation mechanism: bumping the fingerprint string forces full
re-census under a new hash definition without a destructive migration —
confirms the bead's own framing.

**Decision:** shipped the dedup fix now (epoch-free, ~14-16% real CPU cut on
this benchmark, zero behavior change). Did NOT implement merkle or orjson —
both change `session_hash` bytes, which is a durable-evidence epoch per the
consumer map above, and per the lane brief that decision needs coordinator
sign-off, not an autonomous call. Recording the numbers here so that call can
be made with real data instead of estimates: **orjson is the higher-leverage
follow-up** (66-71% vs merkle's 35-37%), and it's simpler to reason about
(one serializer swap vs restructuring what gets hashed) — but it also carries
a distinct risk merkle doesn't: orjson's own byte-output stability
across orjson *library* upgrades isn't guaranteed the way stdlib json's is
(this is literally why `hash_payload`'s docstring already rejects orjson
today). An epoch bump would need to pin the orjson version tightly or accept
periodic re-epochs on orjson upgrades.

**Byte-identity proof:** `tests/unit/pipeline/test_pipeline_ids.py::test_session_revision_projection_golden_hashes`
pins exact hex digests for a fixed session (text + tool_use/tool_result +
attachment + session_event) computed by the NEW dedup implementation;
`test_session_revision_projection_matches_independent_recomputation` inlines
the pre-refactor "build every payload independently" shape and asserts
identical output. Both pass. Also verified interactively pre-commit: the
frozen pre-fix reference implementation (`status_quo_projection` in the
benchmark module) and the patched `session_revision_projection` produce
byte-identical `session_hash`/`message_hashes`/`attachment_hashes`/`event_hashes`
across message counts 1/5/100/300.

**What changed vs what stayed:** `_message_hash_payload`/`_attachment_hash_payload`/
per-event `hash_payload` calls that build the hash-stable payload dicts now
run ONCE per revision (`_session_hash_components`) and are shared by both the
whole-tree hash (`session_content_hash`) and the per-item hashes
(`session_revision_projection`'s message/attachment/event hashes) — previously
each ran twice. The two `hash_payload` calls that do the real O(content)
serialization work (the whole-tree dump for `session_hash`, and the N
per-message dumps for `message_hashes`) are UNCHANGED — both are still
necessary under the current hash definition and are exactly why merkle (which
eliminates the whole-tree dump) and orjson (which speeds up all dumps) are
the bigger, epoch-gated levers above.

AC status: decision recorded (epoch vs cache-first) — landed on "neither, ship
the epoch-free dedup instead" since cache-first gives zero benefit on a cold
full rebuild (nothing cached yet) while dedup gives a real, immediate,
unconditional win; before/after numbers in PR; durable-evidence compatibility
explicitly addressed (see consumer map); no silent identity-hash change
(golden-hash + independent-recomputation tests both pin/prove byte-identity).
